scope: Lemmas 5.1-7.1, Section 8, epsilon ledger, global closure
method: exact symbolic rederivation from the manuscript's definitions

items.claim: E[retained] = (1/q) sum_i C(d_i,2), for a uniformly random injective assignment of the r_p factors to I
items.detail: For a uniformly random injection, each factor F_j lands on a uniformly random v_i, so E|F_j cap E(K[N_sigma(j)])| = (1/q) sum_i |F_j cap E(K[N_i])|. Summing over j and exchanging the order gives (1/q) sum_i sum_j |F_j cap E(K[N_i])|. The r_p factors partition E(K_p), so the inner sum is exactly |E(K[N_i])| = C(d_i,2). Hence the expectation is (1/q) sum_i C(d_i,2) and some assignment attains it. Quantifier check: injectivity needs q >= r_p, which is the stated hypothesis. Edge-disjointness: distinct factors are edge-disjoint in K, and within one factor the retained edges form a matching, so the two K-I edges at a fixed apex are distinct across its triangles.

Substituting sum d_i = qp - M, |E| = C(p,2) + sum d_i, sum C(d_i,2) = (qp^2 - 2pM + S2 - qp + M)/2 and q = 2p - s into Phi <= |E| - (2/q) sum C(d_i,2), then comparing with the manuscript's right-hand side, leaves the difference 0. Every quadratic term in p cancels identically; the residual -s^2/6 and the p/2 are exactly what remains. Note the step ((2p-1)M - S2)/q - M = ((s-1)M - S2)/q uses 2p - 1 - q = s - 1, i.e. the definition of s.

With S2 >= M^2/q, ((s-1)M - S2)/q <= (s-1)y - y^2 where y = M/q. The parabola peaks at y = s/2 - 1/2 with value (s - 1)**2/4. Adding the -s^2/6 of (5.2) gives s**2/12 - s/2 + 1/4 = (s^2 - 6s + 3)/12; the difference from the manuscript's form is 0. The bound is unconditional in M, which is why it closes s = O(sqrt p) with linear error: for s <= c sqrt p the term is (c^2 p + 3)/12 = O(p) = O(n).

items.claim: U = (1/q) sum_e b_e - (delta/(q(q-1))) sum_e b_e(q - b_e)
items.detail: A factor holding e receives one independent vertex with probability 1 - delta and two with probability delta. In the first case e is lost with probability b_e/q; in the second only if both chosen vertices are bad, probability b_e(b_e-1)/(q(q-1)). The mixture minus the manuscript's expression is 0. The algebra turns on (b_e - 1) - (q - 1) = b_e - q, which is where the sign of the gain term comes from. The factor 2 in (5.4) is then forced by Phi = |E| - 2 nu3: a gain of X triangles lowers Phi by 2X.

items.claim: |B_i \ B_j| = a_ij (2(p - |S_j|) - a_ij - 1)/2 with a_ij = |S_i \ S_j|
items.detail: B_i \ B_j is the set of edges of K meeting S_i but not S_j, i.e. the edges of K_p - S_j that meet S_i \ S_j. In a clique on (p - |S_j|) vertices the number of edges meeting a fixed set of size a is C(a,2) + a(p - |S_j| - a); minus the manuscript's closed form this is 0. Monotonicity: with |S_j| <= m and a_ij <= m the bracket is at least 2p - 3m - 1, giving |B_i \ B_j| >= (2p - 3m - 1)/2 * a_ij, and the hypothesis 2p - 3m - 1 >= 0 is exactly what keeps that factor nonnegative.

items.claim: sum_e b_e(q - b_e) = sum over ordered pairs of |B_i \ B_j|
items.detail: Count triples (e,i,j) with e not inside N_i and e inside N_j. For fixed e the number of such pairs is b_e (q - b_e), giving the left side. For fixed (i,j) the number of such e is |B_i \ B_j|, since e not inside N_i means e meets S_i, i.e. e in B_i, and e inside N_j means e not in B_j. Both sides count the same set, so the identity is exact, not an estimate.

items.claim: sum_{i,j} |S_i \ S_j| = (1/2) sum_{i,j} |S_i triangle S_j|
items.detail: Over ORDERED pairs, |S_i triangle S_j| = |S_i \ S_j| + |S_j \ S_i| and the sum is symmetric, so summing the symmetric difference double counts each one-sided difference. Hence the 1/2, and combining with the per-pair bound gives the coefficient (2p - 3m - 1)/4 of (6.2).

items.item: (7.4) and the identity 2 sum beta_i = (2b-1)A_R - A_2R
items.claim: beta_i = C(b,2) - C(b - t_i, 2), and 2 sum_i beta_i = (2b-1)A_R - A_2R
items.detail: The edges of K[Q] available to v_i are those inside N_i cap Q, a set of size b - t_i, so the unavailable count is C(b,2) - C(b - t_i, 2). Expanding twice that gives t_i*(2*b - t_i - 1), and (2b-1)t_i - t_i^2 differs from it by 0. Summing over i replaces t_i by A_R and t_i^2 by A_2R.

items.claim: Phi <= n^2/6 + p/2 - s^2/6 + s rho - 2 rho^2 + kappa_R B_R + ((s - 2 rho - 1)A_R - A_2R)/q
items.detail: Assembling the three families: C(b,2) - (1/r_b) sum_{i not in U} beta_i from QQI, B_U from IRQ, and C(rho,2) - theta_R B_U from RRQ. Choosing U to maximize sum_{i in U} (2 beta_i/r_b + 2(1 - theta_R) g_i) and using 'best u terms >= (u/q) of the total', together with 1 - u/q = r_b/q which turns the coefficient (1 - u/q)/r_b into exactly 1/q, gives nu3 >= C(b,2) + C(rho,2) - (sum beta_i)/q + (u/q)(1 - theta_R) B_R. Then Phi = C(p,2) + sum d_i - 2 nu3 with M = A_R + q rho - B_R, b = p - rho and q = 2p - s. The difference from the manuscript's (7.6) is 0. Two cancellations do the work: (2b-1)A_R/q = ((s-2rho-1)A_R)/q + A_R kills the -A_R coming from sum d_i, and +B_R + (kappa_R - 1)B_R = kappa_R B_R.

items.claim: |L(v_i r)| = b - t_i >= max{rho, u} >= Delta of the gain graph
items.detail: In the gain graph on U x R, deg(v_i) = g_i <= rho because G_i is a subset of R, and deg(r) <= |U| = u. So Delta <= max{rho, u}, and (7.2) supplies b - t_i >= max{rho, u}. Theorem 2.2 is the maximum-degree case of Galvin's theorem, whose hypothesis is |L(e)| >= Delta(B) -- exactly what is available. The colour z of v_i r lies in N_i cap Q, so v_i z is an edge; r z is an edge because K is a clique; v_i r is an edge because r is in N_i. Proper edge colouring makes the resulting IRQ triangles pairwise edge-disjoint.

items.item: Section 7.3 boundary cases rho <= 1 and the theta_R loss
items.claim: loss <= ((rho-1)/b) sum_z |U_z| = theta_R B_U, and rho <= 1 contributes nothing
items.detail: If rho <= 1 then K[R] has no edges, C(rho,2) = 0 and theta_R = max(rho-1,0)/b = 0, so the branch is vacuous and consistent. For rho >= 2: sum_z |U_z| = B_U because each IRQ triangle contributes exactly one used pair (r,z). Injecting the factors of K[R] into the b colours uniformly, a vertex r has degree rho - 1 in K[R], so across all factors at most rho - 1 edges are incident with it; averaging over the injection each is deleted with probability 1/b, giving expected loss at most ((rho-1)/b) sum_z |U_z|. The forbidden-colour deletion is what keeps the RRQ family edge-disjoint from IRQ on the shared edges r z.

items.claim: d(v) > (2n-1)/6 + k and q = o(p) imply eventually d(v) >= 2q + 2
items.detail: With q = o(p) we have n = p + q = (1 + o(1))p, so (2n-1)/6 = (1/3 + o(1))p while 2q + 2 = o(p). Hence the left side exceeds the right for all large members of the sequence. The quantifier is 'eventually along the sequence', which is all the contradiction argument needs.

items.item: Section 8.2 successive matchings, the Dirac hypothesis
items.claim: before choosing M_i the available graph on N_i has min degree >= d_i - i >= d_i/2, so Dirac applies and yields a matching of size floor(d_i/2)
items.detail: Each earlier matching removes at most one edge at any given vertex, so after i-1 steps a vertex of N_i has lost at most i-1 incident edges and retains degree at least (d_i - 1) - (i - 1) = d_i - i. The requirement d_i - i >= d_i/2 is i <= d_i/2, and i <= q with d_i >= 2q + 2 gives d_i/2 >= q + 1 > q >= i. Dirac's hypothesis on the d_i-vertex available graph is min degree >= d_i/2, which is exactly what has been established; a Hamilton cycle yields a matching of size floor(d_i/2) by taking alternate edges. Rounding is accounted for: sum floor(d_i/2) >= (1/2) sum d_i - q/2, which is (8.3).

items.claim: Odd(J) = O, |E(J)| <= p-1, Delta(J) <= 2, and R_1 = R_0 - J has all degrees even
items.detail: For an internal vertex x_j, deg_J(x_j) is the number of the two incident path edges that lie in J, i.e. [prefix(j-1) odd] + [prefix(j) odd]. That is odd exactly when the prefix parity changes at position j, i.e. exactly when x_j is in O. At x_1, deg_J = [prefix(1) odd] = [x_1 in O]. At x_p, deg_J = [prefix(p-1) odd], and since |O| is even by the handshaking lemma, prefix(p-1) is odd exactly when x_p is in O. So Odd(J) = O on both endpoints and inside, which is where the evenness of |O| is actually used. J is a subgraph of a Hamilton path, so |E(J)| <= p - 1 and Delta(J) <= 2, whence delta(R_1) >= p - 1 - q - 2.

items.item: Section 8.3 Turan threshold and the mod-3 correction
items.claim: delta(R_1) > 3p/4 gives a K_5; removing nothing, a C_4 or a C_5 makes |E| divisible by 3 while preserving even degrees
items.detail: A K_5-free graph on p vertices has at most (1 - 1/4)p^2/2 = 3p^2/8 edges by Turan, while delta > 3p/4 forces more than 3p^2/8, so a K_5 exists. Residues: |E(C_4)| = 4 = 1 mod 3 and |E(C_5)| = 5 = 2 mod 3, so removing the C_4 when |E(R_1)| = 1 mod 3 and the C_5 when it is 2 mod 3 lands on 0 mod 3 in both cases, and removing nothing covers 0 mod 3. Every vertex of a cycle loses exactly 0 or 2 incident edges, so evenness of all degrees survives. Both cycles are taken inside one fixed K_5, so only one removal is ever needed.

items.item: (8.9) the 0.91p threshold, and that AX2 is applied on the original p vertices
items.detail: Total degree loss from R_0 to H is at most 2 from J plus 2 from C, i.e. at most 4, giving delta(H) >= p - 1 - q - 4. With q <= p/20 this is at least 0.95p - 5, and 0.95p - 5 >= 0.91p reduces to 0.04p >= 5, i.e. p >= 125 -- comfortably inside 'sufficiently large p'. The threshold identity is exact: 0.9 + eps_0 with eps_0 = 1/100 is 0.91. Crucially |V(H)| = p: the correction deletes EDGES only (the path subgraph J and one cycle C), never a vertex, so the threshold is measured against the original p-vertex clique set and no deletion silently changes it. Total edges removed is at most (p-1) + 5 = p + 4.

items.item: (8.10)-(8.11) the packing count and the final identity
items.detail: The decomposition of H supplies |E(H)|/3 = (C(p,2) - |F| - O(p))/3 triangles on top of the |F| matching triangles, giving nu3 >= (1/3)C(p,2) + (2/3)|F| - O(p). Substituting into Phi = C(p,2) + sum d_i - 2 nu3 and using |F| >= (1/2) sum d_i - q/2 leaves 0 against the manuscript's (1/3)C(p,2) + (1/3) sum d_i. Then sum d_i <= pq, and (1/3)C(p,2) + pq/3 equals (p+q)^2/6 - (p + q^2)/6 identically, difference 0. Since (p + q^2)/6 >= 0 the whole is at most n^2/6, and the error is O(p + q) = O(n). So the sparse regime is closed integrally, with an ABSOLUTE constant, which is what Section 9.2 needs.

items.item: the deletion inequality Phi(G) <= Phi(G - v) + d(v)
items.claim: for every v in I
items.detail: |E(G)| = |E(G - v)| + d(v), and nu3(G) >= nu3(G - v) because any edge-disjoint triangle family of G - v is one of G. Hence Phi(G) = |E(G-v)| + d(v) - 2 nu3(G) <= |E(G-v)| + d(v) - 2 nu3(G-v) = Phi(G-v) + d(v). Deleting a vertex of I leaves a split graph, so the minimal counterexample argument stays inside the class. This is the step the auditor left unverified in the previous run; it is elementary and it holds.

Minimality in the number of vertices means G_k - v is not a counterexample, so Phi(G_k - v) <= (n-1)^2/6 + k(n-1). Combining with the deletion inequality and Phi(G_k) > n^2/6 + k n gives d(v) > [n^2/6 + k n] - [(n-1)^2/6 + k(n-1)] = N/3 + k - 1/6, which is exactly (2n-1)/6 + k; the difference from the manuscript's form is 0. Note this needs I nonempty, which is why the q = 0 case is handled by Section 8 (q = o(p) includes q = 0) rather than by this step.

items.item: n_k -> infinity, and the eventual-to-global closure
items.claim: the sequence of minimal counterexamples has unbounded order, and an eventual bound with an absolute constant contradicts (9.1)
items.detail: For any fixed order n, Phi <= |E| <= C(n,2) < n^2/6 + k n once k > n/2, so no counterexample of bounded order survives all k; hence n_k -> infinity and every 'for sufficiently large n' statement in Sections 4-8 is applicable. Conversely, each regime produces an ABSOLUTE constant C with Phi <= n^2/6 + C n on its cell, so choosing k > C contradicts (9.1) on that cell. Since the cells exhaust all subsequential limits (K-COVER, verified separately), every subsequence is impossible and Theorem 1.1 follows. The formal counterpart global_bound_from_eventual_high_degree implements exactly this shape, converting an eventual bound with constant 2 into Phi <= n^2/6 + max(2, N) n for all split graphs; the max is what absorbs the finitely many orders below the threshold.

items.item: K-EPS, the explicit margin constant c_eps
items.claim: on eps <= alpha <= 2 - eps, mu(alpha) >= c_eps with c_eps = eps^2/48
items.detail: mu is the pointwise minimum of alpha^2/12 and (2-alpha)^2/48 and is therefore minimized on the closed interval at one of its endpoints. At alpha = eps it is epsilon**2/12; at alpha = 2 - eps it is epsilon**2/48. The smaller is epsilon**2/48, so c_eps = eps^2/48 > 0. This is an explicit positive constant depending only on eps, which is what the bulk regime requires.

items.claim: the quadratic margin beats the integrality loss: c_eps p^2 - O(p) - o(n^2) > 0 eventually
items.detail: Losses entering the bulk regime, in order. Theorem 4.2 supplies nu3* >= T(G) + mu(alpha) p^2 - p/4, so the margin is at least eps^2 p^2/48 minus a linear term. Theorem 2.1 costs nu3 >= nu3* - o(n^2). In this regime alpha < 2 gives q < 2p, hence n = p + q < 3p and n^2 < 9p^2, so the o(n^2) loss is also o(p^2): for every c > 0 it is eventually at most c p^2. Choosing c = eps^2/96 leaves a margin of at least eps^2 p^2/48 - eps^2 p^2/96 - p/4 = eps^2 p^2/96 - p/4, which is positive once p > 24/eps^2. So nu3 >= T(G) eventually, contradicting (9.1). Every quantity in the chain is explicit: the only non-effective ingredient is the threshold hidden inside o(n^2), which is exactly the effectivity the manuscript already declares it does not claim in this regime.

items.item: K-EPS, scope of what is being closed
items.claim: this is the MANUSCRIPT's tolerance ledger, not the Lean nibble internals
items.detail: The manuscript uses Theorem 2.1 (Haxell-Rodl/Yuster) as a cited external theorem, so its epsilon ledger is the bookkeeping above: mu(alpha) against o(n^2), plus the explicit constants of Sections 5-8. That ledger is now closed. The Lean development additionally proves an AX1 statement internally through a nibble chain; that chain's own parameter ledger is a different object and is NOT audited here. Since the manuscript's proof depends only on the cited theorem, the manuscript-level claim does not rest on it.
